en: *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra-śāstra-kārikā*,
one fascicle;
composed by Bodhisattva Asaṅga.
One should know that supreme benefit pertains to the body and its dependents;
it consists in the non-retrogression regarding what has been attained and what has not yet been attained, which is called the most excellent entrustment.
It is vast and supreme within the mind, reaching the ultimate state free from inversion.
In the sphere of the altruistic intention for benefit, the virtues of this vehicle are fulfilled.
All six perfections are called "giving," categorized as material, fearlessness, and the Dharma;
herein, one, two, and three are termed the "practice of non-abiding."
To repay the kindness of oneself, one does not cling to any karmic fruition;
to remain free from non-arising, and to remain free from other practices.
Restrained within the three spheres, one eliminates the conceptual mind regarding signs.
All subsequent doubts and perplexities are entirely eliminated as they arise.

If one were to construct [the Buddha] through accumulation, his wondrous marks would not be supreme marks, for they are subject to the three characteristics of change and transformation; one who is free from these is called the Tathāgata.
The profundity of cause and effect was taught during that evil age;
it is not without benefit, owing to the distinction of three types of bodhisattvas.
Because they had previously upheld the training in the precepts under former Buddhas, [they were able to understand it].
Because they have planted roots of goodness, they are said to be endowed with precepts and virtue.
Because they are able to sever the notion of a self and the notion of phenomena, they are said to be endowed with wisdom; thus, two sets of four become eight.
Arising as a distinct entity in succession, it persists until the end of one's lifespan;
seeking further rebirth in other realms, the notion of a self (*ātman*) is fourfold.
Because it is entirely non-existent, it does not exist; because it exists [as a conventional designation], it cannot be said [to exist or not].
Because these are the causes of verbal expression, there are four kinds of conceptualization regarding phenomena (*dharmasaṃjñā*).
Through the power of their faith and understanding: first, by virtue of faith, they give rise to the notion of reality;
second, because they do not grasp things according to their literal expression; and third, because they grasp them as being correctly taught.
The Buddha’s realization of the fruit is not through inference; it is known by means of the knowledge resulting from his vows.
For those who seek profit and honor, he prohibited them from speaking for themselves.
He realized non-abiding in phenomena because he was in accordance with this [truth].
Just as one abandons the raft—this is the intentional meaning (saṃdhāya-bhāṣita) that should be understood.
The emanation-body is not the true Buddha, nor is it the speaker of the Dharma;
the teaching of the Dharma is free from dualistic grasping, and that which is taught transcends all verbal expression.
Speaking for others what one has received for oneself is not without benefit, as it accumulates merit;
yet merit alone does not sustain enlightenment, for those two [merit and wisdom] are able to sustain it.
Because they obtain the cause of the intrinsic nature, these and the rest constitute birth.
Because it is solely the Buddha-dharma, it can accomplish the most supreme merit.
Because it does not grasp at its own fruit, it is neither graspable nor speakable;
because it liberates one from the two obstacles, it is called the "Sublime Birth Free from Dispute."
At the place of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, he spoke of not grasping at the realization of dharmas;
it is through this that the realization of dharmas is accomplished, for it is neither something to be grasped nor something spoken.
The flow of wisdom is the nature of consciousness-only; the buddha-fields are not objects of attachment.
Because it is formless and supreme, it is not adorned, yet its nature is one that permits adornment.
Like Mount Sumeru, it is without grasping in its enjoyment;
because it is not of the nature of outflows (*āsrava*), it is also not produced by causes.
To manifest their many distinctions and to establish their excellence, the preceding and succeeding merits are shown to be different; thus, further analogies are set forth.
Because both are established as venerable, they are distinguished by the excellence of their outflow (*niṣyanda*).
Because it is the cause of afflictions, because it is both inferior and superior,
because its fruit is the suffering of excellence, because the supreme matter is difficult to encounter,
because the shore of the object is unknowable, and because it is not shared with others.
Because this nature is profound, because it excels other abbreviated explanations,
because its lineage is noble and superior, and because its merit is more distinguished than ordinary merit;
when practicing patience, although one undergoes suffering, one practices virtue.
Because his virtue is immeasurable, it is for this reason called a "superior matter.
Since he is free from anger and resentment, it is not of the nature of suffering;
possessing peaceful bliss and great compassion, his actions do not result in the fruit of suffering.
Because the cause for generating the mind is not abandoned, one should therefore seek it with firm resolve;
this refers to the limit of attaining patience (*kṣānti*) as well as the skillful means (*upāya*) of this mind.
One should know that the practitioner of correct conduct acts thus because it is the cause for benefiting sentient beings.
Regarding the characteristics of sentient beings, one should know that they are to be completely dispelled.
Those "beings" are merely aggregates of names; the Supreme Ones eliminate all conceptions thereof.
The World-Honored Ones are peerless, for they are endowed with true vision.
The fruit does not abide in the causal stage; it is the cause for attaining that fruit.
Because the World-Honored One speaks with truthful words, one should know there are four kinds [of teachings]:
establishing essential vows, teaching the Hīnayāna, and teaching the meaning of the Mahāyāna.
Because all prophecies given by the Buddhas are without distinction,
and because one cannot grasp them as being either concordant or not, they are neither real nor false;
yet for those who cling to them according to the literal expression, [the Buddha] spoke in that manner for their sake.
Constantly existing in all places, yet not attained within true nature;
Because of dwelling in ignorance, one fails to dwell in wisdom and thus attains the truth.
Ignorance is like darkness; one should cultivate wisdom so that it is like light.
Because the capacity to counteract and that which is to be remedied, as well as gain and loss, are manifested before one;
through such correct practice, one obtains such a measure of merit.
Now, the functional activity of one who practices correctly according to the Dharma shall be explained.

Regarding persons, there are three types: those who uphold [the teachings], those who hear them extensively explained, and those who attain the meaning through others as well as by means of their own hearing and reflection.
This refers to those who have matured internally; the rest bring others to spiritual maturity.
Due to the greatness of the object, the time, and the nature [of the act], merit is far superior to other merit.
It is not due to the nature of the field, nor its uniqueness;
rather, it is because the one who relies upon it is a Great Being, and because such [teachings] are difficult to hear, the supreme cause increases.
If one merely upholds the True Dharma, the basis of reliance becomes a vessel;
having eliminated all karmic obstructions, one swiftly attains the nature of wisdom and supernormal powers.
Worldly sublime matters are fulfilled, and the resultant maturation is most noble.
One who practices this Dharma should know that such karma is thereby acquired.
When one acts according to one's own [deluded] self, even while claiming to be a bodhisattva,
it is called a "mental obstruction," for it contradicts the mind of non-abiding.
Because the prophecy was granted for a later time, the practice under Dīpaṃkara was not superior;
the Bodhisattva’s practice there was identical, for it was not truly produced by causes.
Since its characteristic is the absence of characteristics, it is revealed to be not false.
Because this Dharma is the Buddha-Dharma, it is entirely devoid of conditioned characteristics.
One should know that the *dharmakāya* Buddha is like a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*),
for his unobstructed and perfectly endowed body is of a pervasive nature.
Furthermore, because the essence of its virtue is great, it is also called the "Great Body.
This body is not a substantial existence; it is said that its activity is non-substantial.
Failing to realize the dharma-realm, one forms the intention to deliver sentient beings.
And purifying the fields of merit—this is called deception and falsehood.
Regarding bodhisattvas and sentient beings, all phenomena lack intrinsic nature;
if one understands this, though not yet a noble one, it should be known as "noble wisdom."
Although one does not perceive any phenomena, this is not because there is no eye;
the Buddha is able to possess the five [eyes] because objects are illusory.
The various mental streams flow on because they are devoid of the foundations of mindfulness.
That which lacks such support does not persist; therefore, it is said to be false.
One should know that this wisdom-support is not false;
because it reveals the cause of merit, its analogy is stated once again.
It is said that within the true dharmakāya, there are no secondary marks of perfection, nor is it possessed of the primary marks;
one should know that its nature is not that of a body.
There is no distinction within the dharmakāya, for the Tathāgata is non-dual.
To emphasize its characteristics: because both entities are non-existent, even the Buddha’s teaching does not exist.
To speak of these two is a conceptual construction;
since they are not separate from the dharmadhātu, even that teaching lacks intrinsic nature.
Although that which speaks and that which is spoken are exceedingly profound, there are nonetheless those who possess reverence and faith;
for it is neither a sentient being nor a non-sentient being, as it accords with the nature of the noble ones.
Because there is no dharma whatsoever that exists, the Unsurpassed Awakening should be known;
because the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) does not increase, it is the nature of pure equality.
Furthermore, it is unsurpassed in terms of skillful means, because its nature is free from outflows (āsrava) and is not a mundane dharma.
Therefore, though it is not a wholesome dharma, it is called "wholesome" by virtue of this.
Although the teaching of the Dharma is indeterminate, one should know that it is not without effect;
by means of this single Jewel of the Dharma, it surpasses those other jewels immeasurably.
Regarding all categories of calculation and estimation, there are likewise differences;
yet when one investigates the world, no analogy can reach it.
Because the Dharma-realm is equal, the Buddha does not deliver sentient beings.
All names converge within them; they do not exist outside the dharma-realm.
If one gives rise to attachment to dharmas, it is the same fault as attachment to a self.
To insistently grasp at sentient beings as being liberated is a false attachment born of non-attachment.
One should not regard the physical form [as the essence], for it is only the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata;
lest that Cakravartin King be deemed equal to the Tathāgata.
Even though he possesses the fruits of the marks and is perfected in merit, such equality is not permitted.
One can realize the Dharmakāya through the distinct nature of skillful means.
Those who merely see forms and hear sounds do not know the Buddha;
this Dharmakāya of True Suchness is not within the realm of consciousness.
That merit shall not be lost, and its retribution shall never cease;
even the attainment of patience shall not be interrupted, for one has attained the stainless state.
To further discuss the causes of merit, I shall now set forth these similes.
Because that merit is without [personal] retribution, it is correctly grasped and not grasped excessively.
That merit brings about the fruit of emanation; performing deeds for the benefit of sentient beings, those activities proceed spontaneously as he attains Buddhahood and manifests in all directions.
Coming and going and so forth are transformations; the Perfectly Awakened One is eternally unmoving.
Within the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), one should know that he is neither identical to nor different from it.
Just as fine dust is used to make ink, this serves as a metaphor to reveal the realm of phenomena.
This treatise describes the making of ink to manifest the exhaustion of afflictions.
Its nature is neither an accumulation nor a collection;
it reveals that its nature is not one, and clarifies that within that collective nature, it is not diverse.
Not understanding that these are merely conventional expressions, the various ordinary fools falsely cling to them;
they negate both self and phenomena because they have not realized awakening.
Therefore, regarding what is seen and what is not seen, they falsely cling to non-existent objects.
Because these are subtle obstacles, they are severed through such knowledge.
By attaining two kinds of wisdom, as well as meditative concentration (*samādhi*), they are then eliminated.
To manifest merit and clarify the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is not without inexhaustible merit.
When the Buddhas preach the Dharma, they do not say that the body is an emanation;
because they do not speak of it as such, this is their true teaching.
The Tathāgata’s realization of nirvāṇa is neither created nor distinct [from it].
This accumulation that constructs existence is ninefold, through observation by means of correct wisdom.
One observes the signs, consciousness, the dwelling place, the body, and enjoyments— those of the past,
those currently existing, and those yet to come— through detailed examination.
Through the observation of characteristics, Regarding experience and flux,
Within conditioned phenomena, One attains stainless mastery.
*Verses from the Commentary on the Diamond Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* (Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra-śāstra-kārikā)
